blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Two models write "the child starts at least two years after its parent" in the aggregated and the cumulative form. Solved as MILPs on the same data, what do they return?

options.text: Different optimal values, since the cumulative form allows fewer plans
options.says: It allows fewer fractional points, not fewer whole plans.

options.text: Different optimal values, since the aggregated form allows more plans
options.says: With binary variables the aggregated form allows exactly the same plans.

options.text: The same optimal value, since the solver rewrites both into one form
options.says: The solver solves what it is given; the forms agree because of the binaries.

options.text: The same optimal value, since with binaries both forms allow the same plans
options.says: Right: the forms differ only for fractional values, which a MILP solution does not have.

origin.section: The Same Rule Can Be Written as One Aggregated Row or as One Row per Year

questions.stem: In an LP relaxation the aggregated form lets a child start in the same year as its parent, although the lag is one year. The child is funded at 0.3. What allowed it?

options.text: The funding row, since a partly funded child needs only a partly funded parent
options.says: The funding row is satisfied either way; it is the timing row's big-M slack that lets the timing slip.

options.text: The lag itself, since one year is too short for the LP to notice
options.says: The cumulative form notices the same one-year lag in the same LP.

options.text: The big-M term, since a partly funded child leaves 0.7 times M of slack
options.says: Right: M(1 - 0.3) is large enough to excuse any start year.

options.text: The objective, since NPV rewards starting the child early
options.says: The objective explains why the LP wants it, not why the rows allow it.

origin.section: Two Forms That Allow the Same Plans Can Have Different LP Bounds

questions.stem: Children in a new portfolio have ten-year windows. A colleague keeps the aggregated precedence form because it needs only two rows per child. What should you do first?

options.text: Measure both forms' row counts and keep the smaller one
options.says: Size alone does not decide; a weaker bound can make the search far longer.

options.text: Keep the aggregated form, since both return the same plan
options.says: The same plan, but possibly after a much longer search; the bound is what differs.

options.text: Keep the aggregated form, since big-M rows solve faster
options.says: Big-M rows weaken the LP bound; nothing makes them cheaper to solve.

options.text: Measure both forms' LP bounds and solve times on this data
options.says: Right: the cumulative form costs ten rows per child here, and only a measurement says whether a tighter bound pays for them.

origin.section: Disaggregated Is Stronger, Not Always Bigger

concepts: which plans the aggregated and cumulative forms allow
why the aggregated form's LP bound is weaker
